title: Photo sharing
summary: Direct uploads, media processing and CDN delivery.
prompt: Design a photo-sharing service: users upload photos, which are resized and shown to followers in a profile grid and on a photo page. Focus on upload and delivery, not the feed ranking.

requirements: Functional: upload a photo with a caption, view it in several sizes, list a user’s photos newest first, delete.
Non-functional: uploads succeed on flaky mobile networks; viewing is fast worldwide; photos are never lost once acknowledged.
estimation: 10M uploads a day ≈ 115/s average; peaks of ~500/s.
Original ~3 MB plus ~4 resized variants totalling ~1 MB ≈ 4 MB per photo ≈ 40 TB a day ≈ 14.6 PB a year.
Views outnumber uploads by orders of magnitude, so delivery is a CDN problem.
api: POST /uploads → {uploadId, presignedUrl}: the client uploads bytes directly to object storage, in parts if large.
GET /users/{id}/photos?cursor= and GET /photos/{id} → metadata plus CDN URLs per size.
data: photos(photo_id, owner_id, caption, status, created_at, variants) keyed for “by owner, newest first”.
Object storage keys like originals/{photoId} and variants/{photoId}/{size}.webp; objects are immutable.
Use time-sortable IDs (for example a timestamp-prefixed ID) so pagination is a cursor on the ID.
design: Upload: API issues a presigned URL → client uploads straight to object storage → client confirms → a processing job is queued.
Workers strip EXIF location data, generate variants, and mark the photo ready.
Delivery: clients load variants from a CDN that pulls from object storage; metadata comes from the API, with a cache for hot profiles.
deepDives: Presigned direct uploads keep large bodies off the app servers; multipart uploads allow resuming after a dropped connection.
Immutable, content-addressed or versioned URLs allow very long CDN cache lifetimes; deletion removes the metadata and purges or lets objects expire.
Durability: acknowledge only after storage confirms the write; object storage replicates across zones.
bottlenecks: Processing backlog during peaks: autoscale workers on queue depth; show the original until variants are ready.
Storage cost: move cold originals to cheaper tiers and serve resized variants.
Abuse: scan uploads for prohibited content before they become public.
tradeoffs: Generating variants eagerly costs storage; resizing on demand at the edge saves storage but adds first-view latency.
Eventual readiness (processing state) in exchange for fast uploads.
Stripping location metadata protects privacy but loses data some users want.

rubric.text: Uploaded bytes directly to object storage rather than through app servers.
Processed media asynchronously with a queue and workers.
Served images from a CDN with long-lived immutable URLs.
Separated metadata storage from blob storage.
Estimated storage growth and named cost controls.
Supported resumable uploads and acknowledged only durable writes.
